edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), De poenitentia, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Plerosque tamen hoc opus, ut publicationem sui, aut suffugere, aut de die in diem differre, praesumo; pudoris magis memores quam salutis: velut illi, qui in partibus verecundioribus corporis contracta vexatione, conscientiam medentium vitant, et ita cum erubescentia sua pereunt. Intolerandum scilicet pudori, Domino offenso satisfacere, saluti prodactae reformari. Nae tu verecunda bonus, ad delinquendum expandens frontem, ad deprecandum vero subducens. Ego rubori locum non facio, cum plus de detrimento ejus acquiro, cum ipse hominem quodammodo exhortatur, Ne me respexeris, dicens, per te mihi melius est perire. Certe periculum ejus tunc, si forte, onerosum est, cum penes insultaturos in risiloquio consistit, ubi de alterius ruina alter attollitur, ubi prostrato superscenditur. Caeterum inter fratres atque conservos, ubi communis spes, metus, gaudium, dolor, passio (quia communis spiritus de communi Domino et Patre), quid tu hos aliud quam te opinaris? Quid consortes casuum tuorum, ut plausores, fugis? Non potest corpus de unius membri vexatione laetum agere: condoleat universum, et ad remedium conlaboret, necesse est. In uno et altero Ecclesia est, Ecclesia vero Christus. Ergo cum te ad fratrum genua protendis, Christum contrectas, Christum exoras. Aeque illi cum super te lacrymas agunt, Christus patitur, Christus Patrem deprecatur. Facile impetratur semper, quod filius postulat. Grande plane emolumentum verecundiae occultatio delicti pollicetur. Videlicet si quid humanae notitiae subduxerimus, proinde et Deum celabimus? Adeone existimatio hominum et Dei conscientia comparantur? An melius est damnatum latere, quam palam absolvi? Miserum est sic ad Exomologesin pervenire. Malo enim ad miseriam pervenitur, sed ubi poenitendum est deserit miserum: quia factum est salutare. Miserum est secari et cauterio exuri, et pulveris alicujus mordacitate cruciari: tamen quae per insuavitatem medentur, et emolumento curationis offensam sui excusant, et praesentem injuriam superventurae utilitatis gratia commendant.
pass_a_gloss: Most people, however, I suppose this work, as a publication of themselves, either to flee or to differ from day to day; more mindful of shame than of salvation: just like those who, in the more shameful parts of the body, having contracted vexation, avoid the consciousness of healers, and thus perish with their own shame. It is certainly intolerable to shame, to satisfy the Lord who has been offended, to be reformed for salvation that has been betrayed. Behold, you are shamefaced, good, expanding your forehead to sin, but withdrawing it to deprecate. I do not give place to blushes, since I acquire more from the loss of it, when he himself exhorts man in a way, saying, Do not look back at me, saying, it is better for me to perish through you. Certainly, his danger is then, if perhaps, burdensome, when it consists among those who insult in ridicule, where one is lifted up at the ruin of another, where one is trampled upon when prostrated. Meanwhile, among brothers and fellow servants, where there is common hope, fear, joy, sorrow, passion (because there is a common spirit from the common Lord and Father), what do you think of these other than yourself? What do you flee from these companions of your misfortunes, as if they were applauding? The body cannot be happy about the vexation of one of its members: it is necessary for the whole to sympathize and to labor towards a remedy. The Church is in one and another, and the Church is truly Christ. Therefore, when you stretch out to the knees of brothers, you touch Christ, you beseech Christ. Similarly, when they shed tears over you, Christ suffers, Christ beseeches the Father. What the son asks is always easily obtained. The hiding of sin certainly promises a great advantage of shame. Evidently, if we have withdrawn something from human knowledge, we will also hide it from God? Are the estimation of men and the consciousness of God compared? Is it better to be damned in secret than to be absolved in public? It is wretched to come to confession in this way. For misery is approached, but where there is need to repent, misery is abandoned: because it has become salvation. It is wretched to be cut and to be burned by a cauter, and to be tormented by the biting of some powder: yet those things that heal through unpleasantness, and excuse their own offense by the benefit of the cure, and commend the present injury for the sake of future utility.
pass_b_english: I suspect most people treat this work as a public exposure of themselves and either flee from it or put it off day after day; they care more about saving face than saving their souls. They act just like patients who contract a disease in the shameful parts of the body, avoid the doctor's scrutiny, and die of their own embarrassment. It is simply intolerable that shame should block us from satisfying the offended Lord and being restored to a salvation we have betrayed. So you're modest, are you? — bold enough to bare your forehead when sinning, but suddenly shy when it's time to beg forgiveness. I make no room for blushes, because I gain more from their loss; shame itself exhorts a person, saying, 'Don't look at me; it's better for me to perish through you.' That danger becomes oppressive only when it lodges among mockers who trade in ridicule, where one man rises on another's ruin and climbs over the prostrate. But among brothers and fellow servants, where hope, fear, joy, sorrow, and passion are shared — because a common Spirit flows from our common Lord and Father — what do you take these people for except yourself? Why flee the companions of your own misfortunes as if they were there to applaud? A body cannot rejoice when one member suffers; the whole must sympathize and work together for a cure. The Church exists in each and every member, and the Church is Christ. Therefore, when you stretch yourself out at the brothers' knees, you touch Christ and beseech Christ. And when they shed tears over you, Christ suffers and Christ intercedes with the Father. What the Son asks is always granted with ease. The concealment of sin promises a great payoff for shame. Obviously, if we hide something from human knowledge, we think we'll hide it from God too? Do we really equate human opinion with God's conscience? Is it better to be damned in secret than absolved in public? It is wretched to come to confession like this. For you approach misery, but right where repentance is needed, you abandon misery — because it has become salvation. It is wretched to be cut, burned with a cautery, tormented by biting powder; yet the things that heal through unpleasantness excuse their own offense by the benefit of the cure, and they commend the present injury for the sake of future utility.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal gloss, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that preserves all theological and rhetorical distinctions. Specifically, the complex metaphor of the medical treatment (cautery and powder) and the Christological connection to the Church are handled correctly in both. The translation of 'Exomologesin' as 'confession' is appropriate for the context.
